title: I Learned in a Due Process Hearing That the Accommodations Never Happened
author: Larry J. Walsh
summary: A former principal recounts a three-day due process hearing over a seventh grader's IEP, where he discovered that four of the six accommodations he had signed off on never happened in any classroom. Teachers testified they had been handed eleven IEPs at once, filed them in a folder and never knew what applied to their students. The author lays out the competing pressures: a lawyer pushing a quick legal settlement, a case manager who had done what she was told, defensive teachers with forty-plus plans and no time to read them, and a mother who simply wanted her son served. After settling with eighty hours of compensatory tutoring, he told the mother the plan was right and the school had failed to carry it out. That summer he rebuilt how plans reach classrooms with one-page summaries per student, ten-minute case manager walkthroughs and six-week classroom checks. The transferable lesson is that a signature on a plan is a legal promise, and a leader must build a system that verifies it is kept.
points: A signed IEP is not implemented until each teacher knows, in plain language, what each student needs, and someone checks that it happens.
Handing a new teacher a stack of IEPs at one meeting, with no protected time to read them, predictably produces compliance on paper and failure in classrooms.
The fix was practical: one-page student summaries tied to the class roster, early walkthroughs by case managers, and six-week classroom visits with a simple form.
Owning the failure directly with the family mattered, and the mother's question about the next kid is the standard leaders should hold themselves to.
Leaders should look for implementation gaps themselves, early and often, and tell families before an advocate does.
quotes: I was thinking about a twelve-year-old who had spent seven months in rooms where the adults did not know what he needed, while his mother trusted the paper I had signed. A signature on a plan is not a plan in the classroom.
She said she had been handed eleven IEPs on the same day, during the same meeting, and had put them in a folder.
The teachers were defensive. They had forty-plus IEPs and 504 plans in their rosters and no protected time to read them.
I told her we had failed her son. I told her the plan was right and we had not done it.

No more handing teachers eleven IEPs in one meeting. Each teacher got a one-page summary for each student, three to five accommodations in plain language, attached to their class roster in the grading system.
The six-week classroom checks found gaps every year I was there. Fewer every year. Never zero.
Do not wait for an advocate to show you where the gaps are. Go look for them yourself, early and often, and when you find one, tell the family before they find it for you.
